claims.text: The investigated material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The starting alloy retains an fcc matrix.
The starting alloy has notable formability, strength, and fatigue performance.
Degradation under oxidizing conditions is governed by selective oxidation kinetics.
Oxidizing exposure produces a non-uniform, non-protective oxide scale.
Chromium and titanium oxidize faster than aluminum in this alloy under the proposed oxidizing conditions.
Preferential oxidation of chromium and titanium relative to aluminum causes an inhomogeneous, porous, and poorly adherent scale.
The defective oxide scale fails to protect the substrate.
Poor scale quality promotes spallation and interfacial degradation.
Low oxygen availability in reducing environments limits external oxide-scale formation.
Reducing exposure permits internal oxidation, oxygen penetration, and near-interface defect accumulation.
Oxidizing exposure will produce more scale heterogeneity, spallation, and interfacial defects than the inert baseline.
Reducing exposure will produce minimal external scale but more internal oxygen penetration and defect accumulation than the inert baseline.
The underlying fcc matrix will remain largely intact unless surface or interface degradation becomes extensive.
At the same elevated temperatures, inert-atmosphere controls will show minimal oxidation and conserved microstructural integrity.
Inert-atmosphere controls will possess stable oxide layers.
A transition between protective-scale behavior or scale absence and scale breakdown occurs approximately within 700–900°C as oxygen partial pressure changes.
Formation of a uniform, adherent, protective scale without significant interfacial defects under oxidizing exposure would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Failure of reducing exposure to produce the predicted internal-defect difference relative to the inert control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis broadly predicts a non-protective scale under oxidizing conditions, whereas the boundary allows oxidizing conditions within the stated regime to produce a protective scale without specifying the compositional, temperature, or oxygen-partial-pressure subrange where that alternative is expected.
